title: Researcher-in-the-loop
text:
Researcher-in-the-loop

A model for AI-enabled UX research where the researcher governs.

For a few years now, the UX research field has been arguing with itself over whether AI is coming to replace us or whether AI can’t do “real” research and we need to hold the line. Is AI coming to replace us? Should we use AI to automate research? Can AI conduct “real” research? Research is about asking questions. However, we can ask better questions about AI in UXR.

We don’t need to ask whether AI can do research. It’s already doing it, and it’s doing it in your org right now, whether or not a researcher is involved. Product managers are pasting interview notes into a model and asking AI to “find themes.” Designers are generating synthetic feedback on wireframes. Executives are asking a chatbot what users think. Research is being democratized whether we govern it or not.

So the real question is: when everyone can do research, who keeps it honest?

Who governs UX research? Who governs AI?

“What if, instead of thinking of automation as the removal of human involvement from a task, we imagined it as the selective inclusion of human participation?” Stanford University HAI

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) AI emerged to keep human judgment inside automated systems, catching the bias, opacity, and plain mistakes that models produce on their own, especially in the ambiguous or rare cases they handle worst. The idea is a feedback loop: human corrections train the system over time. At its best, HITL pairs what AI excels at (pattern recognition, speed, scale) with what humans excel at (ethics, oversight, judgment). But it has a known limit: even when it’s well-designed, a human can become overloaded, checking more than they can meaningfully assess.

Many argue for stepping beyond the human-in-the-loop concept. Konstantinos Lazaros et al., after reviewing 182 peer-reviewed studies, suggest more “sophisticated ‘human-with-the-loop’” partnerships that would adjust the amount of control the human and the AI have based on risk and uncertainty. Rahwan argues that AI systems ultimately require “society-in-the-loop” to negotiate values.

I propose a model I’ve come to call researcher-in-the-loop. It’s a deliberate inversion of “human-in-the-loop,” where a person checks the machine’s work case by case. That model doesn’t scale. It assumes the machine is the researcher and the human is the safety net. Let’s flip that. The researcher isn’t the safety net. The researcher is the person who designs and governs the system and conducts high-risk, high-priority research so that everyone else can conduct research safely, rigorously, and honestly, with escalation engineered into the tools themselves.

This model didn’t come from nowhere.

Three ideas hold it up:

1. Research democratization: The now-familiar argument, articulated clearly by Kara Pernice at Nielsen Norman Group, is that non-researchers can and should do research, but only when it “is accompanied by due diligence: setting guidelines, educating others, and demystifying the process”. Democratization with guardrails is the parent of everything here.

2. ResearchOps: Kate Towsey and the ResearchOps Community gave us the language of research as infrastructure, “the people, mechanisms, and strategies that set user research in motion” (Writing@TeamReOps). What I call governance is really ResearchOps pointed at AI.

3. Atomic research: Daniel Pidcock’s model, alongside Tomer Sharon’s parallel “nuggets,” breaks research into small, tagged, evidence-traceable units. You cannot build a trustworthy, sourced research assistant on top of PDFs buried in a drive; you can only build one on top of atomic, linked evidence.

Everything below is an attempt to assemble those three into a single governance stance. The assembly is the only part I’d claim as mine.

What I learned by saying no

A few years ago, I directed research on a flagship AI-assisted feature that was on a fast track to release. The research told a blunt story: 75% of users could not complete the feature’s core task. The workflow was confusing, the AI was hard to understand and hard to trust, and, most importantly, it didn’t align with what we already knew about how our users wanted to use AI.

This was AI in a B2B product for highly regulated industries (think healthcare, legal, insurance, compliance, security, data privacy, banking). Our users’ working lives were built around transparency, confidentiality, ethical walls, and defensibility. They do not want a black box. They are trained to distrust an answer they can’t trace. An AI feature that couldn’t show its reasoning, couldn’t cite its basis, and couldn’t be verified was culturally incompatible with the people it was built for.

The research surfaced that mismatch, and the decision was a no-go. It reshaped how the company thought about future AI investment.

We all have these war stories. This one contains the entire thesis of this article in miniature. Ungoverned AI is dangerous. It is even more dangerous in high-trust domains. We didn’t catch this because we used a smarter AI model. The researcher caught the failure because of their judgment about risk, confidence, and how real users actually build trust [i]. This is researcher-in-the-loop.

Everything I’m about to propose is an attempt to take that judgment and build it into the system so it fires early and automatically, instead of heroically and late.

That instinct, the one that caught a 75% failure rate, is what we need to preserve. But what if we engineer it into the tools everyone uses?

The two artifacts, in brief

In the researcher-in-the-loop model, most day-to-day research questions don’t go to a researcher at all. They go to governed AI tools. Two such tools I’ve been building are the Librarian and the Persona.

The AI Librarian is your organization’s memory of what you already know about users. Ask it any question, and it pulls from every study, report, and transcript in the governed “library” to give you an executive summary, the sources behind it, and a confidence rating for the answer. Its most valuable response is “We don’t have enough research to answer that.”

The AI Personas are living, conversational representations of your users, built from real qualitative and quantitative research and continuously updated as new data comes in. Anyone can “chat” with a persona to get a quick directional signal. When the data doesn’t support a confident answer, the persona says so and points you toward the researcher and the real research you’d need.

Governance by design; Rigor you don’t have to remember

In most orgs, research quality depends on a researcher being in the room. Remove the researcher, and quality becomes a hope. The researcher-in-the-loop model refuses that fragility. Rigor stops being a manual review step you might get to. It’s engineered into the tools. It is the default.

Recent critiques by Papangelis, Scaff, and Anastasiou & De Liddo warn of a “Synthetic Persona Fallacy,” where black-box tools systematically smooth out human variance and hallucinate confidence. Our model addresses this fragility by making transparency a technical constraint through mandatory sourcing, confidence ratings, and escalation triggers. Three mechanisms carry most of the weight:

  • Mandatory sourcing. No insight without its basis. Every answer traces back to the studies behind it. This is the transparency that our stakeholders, our teams, and our users demand and deserve.
  • Confidence and trust ratings. Every insight carries a signal of how much to lean on it. High-confidence answers move fast. Low-confidence answers slow down and flag themselves.
  • Escalation triggers. The system knows what it can’t handle and automatically pings a human researcher, especially in high-risk and low-confidence areas. Escalation becomes a reflex, not a courtesy or a gatekeeper.

That last mechanism is what moves this from a disclaimer to a governance system. A disclaimer says, “verify important results.” A governance system identifies the important results and routes them to a human before anyone acts on them.

The envelope of replaceability: When AI can stand in and when it can’t

“Success [with AI] requires best practices — loosely held.” Figma’s 2025 AI report

With researcher-in-the-loop AI governance, AI personas, and the AI Librarian, AI can genuinely replace some early research. Not researchers. Not for all the research. But it can replace specific slices of it, and only inside a governed envelope.

To do this with rigor, we don’t default to replacement. Replacing any research is a privilege the system earns, question by question, based on two axes: risk and confidence.

Another way to say this: the model is a way to rightsizing research. Our field has argued for rightsizing for decades. Jakob Nielsen made the case respectable back in 2000, when he told us to “distribute your budget for user testing across many small tests instead of blowing everything on a single, elaborate study.” His “just enough” argument was never really about the number five; it was about matching research effort to the stakes of the question. The envelope does the same thing for the AI era, only now the scarce resource we’re rationing isn’t sample size; it’s human oversight. We spend it where risk and uncertainty are highest, and we don’t waste it where the answer is already clear.

This matrix is the operational heart of the model. It’s whiteboard-simple on purpose, because it has to work as policy, not philosophy. A designer asking, “What have users said about our onboarding tone?” is low-risk and high-confidence, so we let them self-serve. A PM asking a persona to greenlight a launch is off the map entirely (as this is not a low-confidence answer, but a question that isn’t the persona’s to answer at all).

The 75%-failure feature lives in the bottom-right cell. High-risk domain, low real-world confidence in users' trust in the AI. That is the cell where a human researcher must be in the loop, and the cell where a well-governed AI should raise its hand early rather than letting the feature sail toward release.

The loop that improves itself

So far, I’ve described the matrix as if it were a gate: a question comes in, you classify it, you route it once. That’s the tidy version. The real thing is a loop.

Because every time the matrix escalates a high-risk, low-confidence question to the STOP cell, the question is brought to the research team, and a researcher may conduct real research with real users. The research doesn’t just answer its own question and disappear. It goes back into the artifacts. The persona is updated based on what we heard. The Librarian gets a new source to cite. The confidence score on that whole class of questions moves. The next person who asks the persona something adjacent gets a better, better-grounded answer than they would have last week.

That changes what the AI tools are. They’re not a replacement for the research cycle sitting off to one side. They’re one governed step inside it, the fast, cheap, self-serve front door, wired to the slow, deep, human work by a feedback loop.

This is continuous discovery with a governance layer bolted on. Teresa Torres defines the practice as engaging with customers “at least weekly, minimizing the number of decisions they make without customer input.” I want to be honest about the tension there: she keeps a human in weekly contact with real people, while my loop puts an AI at the front door. That’s exactly why the governance layer matters. The self-serve tools make “continuous” cheap; the matrix and the loop are what keep “minimizing decisions made without customer input” from becoming “minimizing contact with customers.” Cheap directional signals move early and stay continuous; expensive, real research is reserved and aimed precisely where the matrix says it’s needed. Research stops being the “bottleneck” it gets called in lower-maturity orgs, where it’s treated as an add-on rather than a necessity, and becomes a resource you deploy where the loop tells you it’ll change the outcome.

This has a consequence I didn’t expect until I watched it happen: the low-confidence cells can become your research backlog. The system tells you where it’s weakest, which is exactly where a human should be looking next. And because each real study raises the confidence ceiling of the artifacts, research spend compounds instead of depreciating; a study you run today keeps paying off in every future query it touches. That compounding isn’t automatic, though: users change and products change, so the artifacts need pruning and expiry dates as much as they need new inputs, or yesterday’s confident answer quietly becomes today’s stale one. Maintained honestly, though, research spend builds on itself instead of evaporating, and for anyone who has ever had to defend a research budget, that’s not a small thing.

The loop can also be part of a bigger loop. The AI artifacts work best in an iterative process. Start with AI. Ask the AI persona about the concept. Have the AI librarian pull everything we have on the topic and what we have learned, thus giving us the grounding.

But a loop that feeds itself can also fool itself. If the artifact shapes which questions get asked, and those questions shape at least some of the research conducted, and that research feeds back into the artifact, you can build a machine that keeps confirming what it already believes and never goes looking in its own blind spots. Iteration sharpens calibration, but it can slowly starve discovery of the unknown-unknowns. So, the loop needs one more guardrail, and it’s a human one: the researcher has to force exploratory research periodically; the system would never request it and would deliberately study the areas where the persona is most confident, not just where it’s uncertain, precisely to catch the places it’s confidently wrong. The loop improves itself. It does not police itself. That part is still the researcher’s job.

Where this breaks

Few models are honest about their own failure points, so let me be honest about mine. A governance system that sounds rigorous can fail in exactly the ways it claims to prevent, and two failure modes worry me most. Both come from the same place: the moment a number or a confident-sounding answer stops being treated as a signal and starts being treated as the truth.

Automation creep and bias: Research by Parasuraman & Manzey, among others, has found that humans systematically over-trust automated output and under-scrutinize it relative to their own judgment, leading to omission and commission errors even among experts. According to Mosier, Skitka, and Burdick, this bias “cannot be prevented by training or instructions.” This is a fear many of us share, especially amid the democratization of research through AI. We don’t want a stakeholder, or even a researcher, to overtrust AI artifacts. This is why the escalation triggers exist. The AI artifacts are designed to tell you how trustworthy the output is. While this may not eliminate automation bias, it should decrease its likelihood and strength.

But this exposes the model’s central risk, and I want to name it plainly: the envelope only works if a question is classified correctly, and classification itself is a judgment call. If the person using the model for self-service is the one deciding whether their question is “high risk” or “low confidence,” you’ve handed the label to exactly the person most motivated to under-rate the risk and get a fast answer, and, thanks to automation bias, least likely to notice they’ve done it.

The same trap applies to the AI itself: a model asked to rate its own confidence is often confidently wrong. Chhikara and others document that LLMs overstate their certainty in ways that misalign with their actual accuracy, which is precisely the risk when someone acts on the rating. The classification can’t rely on the asker’s or the model’s self-report. It has to be engineered into the system, with confidence derived from the underlying research (how much real evidence exists, how recent it is, how consistent it is), not from how sure the model sounds; risk thresholds set in advance by the researcher, not chosen in the moment by whoever wants the answer. The model doesn’t remove that judgment. It moves it upstream to the researcher who defines the rules, keeping it out of the hands of the person with a deadline. Get that wrong and the whole envelope collapses into theater. That is the thing the researcher is really governing.

A thing with numbers: Erika Hall warns us to beware of research theater and false objectivity: rigor comes from discipline and honesty, she argues, not the mere presence of numbers. As she puts it, “just because a thing has numbers doesn’t make it magically objective or meaningful.” My artifacts are built on exactly the thing she’s suspicious of. A confidence rating is “a thing with numbers,” and, paired with automation bias, it’s a prime candidate for manufacturing false objectivity, making a shaky answer feel settled because it arrived with a percentage attached.

So does the model answer Hall? Partly, and only conditionally. Governance can keep the number accountable: every rating traceable to the research behind it, labeled as a signal rather than a verdict, and flagged when the evidence is thin. That’s discipline made structural instead of hoped-for. But it doesn’t make the number “objective,” and I don’t want to pretend it does. A well-sourced confidence rating can still be misread as more certain than it is; that’s a limit of how humans read numbers, not a flaw I can engineer away. Hall’s pressure doesn’t lift once you add governance. It just moves on to the researcher, who has to keep auditing whether the confidence the system projects is confidence it has actually earned.

Notice that neither of these failures is a bug you can patch. Automation bias is a documented feature of how humans treat machines, and false precision is baked into any number that looks more certain than it is. Governance doesn’t eliminate these risks; it can only manage them, and only if the system is built and maintained honestly. That “if” is doing a lot of work, and it’s precisely why the model can’t run on autopilot. Which brings us back to the one component no rating or trigger can replace: the researcher.

The researcher’s new job: From “bottleneck” to governor

“The more advanced the systems become, the more important empathy, context, and ethics feel.” Sophia Omarji

If the tools handle the low-risk, high-confidence middle of the workload, what is the researcher for?

More than ever, the researcher enters the loop wherever expertise is non-negotiable:

  • High-priority, high-impact studies, and key clients or sensitive user groups
  • Discovery and exploratory research, the generative, ambiguous work that can’t be templatized
  • Anything touching protected data, risky populations, or unclear or inappropriate goals
  • Hard questions the tools flag as beyond their envelope
  • Iteration for steering the loop itself, deciding when the AI artifacts are grounded enough to answer, when a question needs a fresh round of real research, and when to force exploratory studies in the areas the tools are most confident about, precisely to catch where they’re confidently wrong.

This is the part I care about most: the researcher is a quality authority over the process itself, not just a reviewer of outputs. The researcher checks that the plan makes sense for the question, that the script and survey items are well-formed, that the method fits, that the analysis is sound, and that stakeholder conversations haven’t biased the work. The AI can draft a study. Only a researcher can confirm it’s the right study, designed correctly, and rigorous enough to bet on.

That is not a diminished role. It’s a promoted one. This researcher stops being the “bottleneck” designers and PMs complain about and becomes the governor of a research system that serves the whole organization. This also means researchers spend fewer hours moderating routine sessions and more hours setting standards, auditing rigor, designing guardrails, and doing the hard, generative research only a human can do.

The anxious question we have been asking, “Will AI replace researchers?” has it backward. AI raises the value of the person who can govern it.

Keep the researcher in the loop

Democratization and rigor are usually sold as a trade-off: let more people do research, accept lower quality. The researcher-in-the-loop model rejects that trade. Governance by design, mandatory sources, honest confidence, automatic escalation, and roles bounded by the norms we already hold let us scale access without scaling risk.

The researcher doesn’t disappear in this future. The researcher doesn’t fight it, either. The researcher governs it. The researcher treats the persona like the user it represents, treats the Librarian like the SME they are, and steps personally into the loop wherever the stakes, the ambiguity, or the craft demand a human who knows better.

This takes AI from a tool to a stance. This is the stance our field needs to take before the question of who keeps research honest gets answered for us.

Let’s build this together

I’m developing the researcher-in-the-loop model in the open, and I want to pressure-test it against how the rest of you are actually working. So, a few honest questions for you:

· If you lead research: Where would you draw the human line? Which cell of that matrix keeps you up at night? What have you already tried to democratize, and what broke?

· If you’re a designer, PM, or founder: What would you want to ask an AI librarian or a persona tomorrow morning? What would make you trust the answer?

· If you build these tools: What would it take to make “insufficient data” and automatic escalation first-class features instead of afterthoughts?

Drop your take in the responses, or reach me directly. I read every message, and the best refinements to this model will come from people living the trade-offs, not from those theorizing about them. If this framing was useful, follow along; I’ll be sharing the templates, escalation rules, and governance patterns as I put them into practice.

The researcher stays in the loop. Let’s make sure the loop is one worth being in.

title: Sterling Cooper built your UX process. We need to redefine it in the age of AI and systems.
text:
Sterling Cooper built your UX process. We need to redefine it in the age of AI and systems.

The rituals of the 1960s ad shop — the whiskey, the pitch room, the account man, the campaign— still shape how UX teams fail in many environments. We have to change that.

Auteur: a film director who holds primary creative control and stamps a distinct, recognizable personal style, vision, and thematic focus across a body of work, much like a novelist or painter.

Walk into a mid-century advertising office and you would see the whole apparatus of modern creative work already assembled: the pitch room, the account man, the campaign, the auteur with the corner office.

I can almost remember the smell of peaty whiskey and stale cigarettes from one of the my favorite shows ever, Mad Men, and I also recall how it characterized advertising in a way that many agencies did for user experience.

And that stung.

https://medium.com/media/5977678cd2e937c6de65da53d7ee8211/href

Decades later, when user experience needed a business to belong to and a way to look serious, it borrowed the entire kit — the deck, the client, the reveal, the portfolio showcase.

We inherited the craft, and the habits bundled with it.

Agency work isn’t what I like doing and you might see some of the framing here; I also believe UX deserves a better future and the numbers prove the value.

Design creates real, measurable outcomes when the right choices land in front of users and organizations: McKinsey’s research on the business value of design found that the strongest design performers posted 32 percentage points higher revenue growth and 56 points higher shareholder returns than their peers over five years, mainly with in house teams.

And at a time where the cost of execution drops like a rock, the right decisions matter more than ever.

That value appears only where design understands the domain, is measured like revenue, integrated across the business, and iterated with real users over time.

Embedded so everyone could learn together.

That approach is precisely why many agencies are not built to sustain when the project goes out for request for proposal. The pitch, the account, the campaign, the auteur, and the revolving door gave UX its polish and quietly hollowed out its practice in a time when product is king.

I’m saying for a lot of work that the giants did was valuable and we still use it today; however it might not be the model we should move forward with.

David Ogilvy built his agency on research-driven, respectful persuasion — the long copy and big idea that treated readers as intelligent. Jay Chiat championed creative risk and account planning, giving strategy a seat beside art.

Together they proved advertising could be both disciplined and daring, reshaping how agencies think, sell, and create. But even Ad Week pointed out in 2019 the hero culture and operating model was shifting before generative AI took a seat.

Their approach does have it place and many UX professionals have adopted them; however they may no longer apply when generative AI can make the artifacts in minutes or billable hours disappear in value based billing.

Here are the outcomes we have to change — it’s no longer acceptable in many cases to talk about the potential where there’s no tangible outcomes, especially if projects go on for a very long time and a lot of money has been spent.

The prestige of that lineage is real but now outdated, which is exactly why almost nobody names the cost to where we are at today.

Hype Over Practice

The most famous scene in Mad Men is a pitch.

A creative director stands in a darkened room clicks through a slide projector, and turns a piece of hardware into a time machine — reframing a product nobody needed as a vehicle for nostalgia to remember times that have gone by, like a magical time machine.

https://medium.com/media/f1f6fb5e4186f8424ec41ab4d39ec215/href

The wheel.

“It’s not called the Wheel. It’s called a Carousel. It lets us travel the way a child travels. Around and around, and back home again… to a place where we know we are loved…Technology is a glittering lure. But he also talked about a deeper bond with the product: nostalgia. It’s delicate but potent.”

This is a masterclass in selling a dream and it is also the original sin.

The room learns that the performance is the product, the applause is the deliverable, and the user has been sold a bill of goods that will never be delivered. Those masterclasses are over at Entertainment Weekly — it’s a great read, but it can show that selling a dream can sometimes be more important than delivery itself.

UX absorbed that lesson completely.

We learned to optimize for the pitch: the big presentation, the polished prototype, the file that photographs well on a Tuesday but has aged poorly by Friday.

The unglamorous practice we should be striving for as practictioners— the eighth usability session, the accessibility fix nobody claps for, the maintenance that keeps a system honest, the focus on affordances that can change the lives of user — has no stage and earns no ovation, and that’s where real user value is.

It’s the selling of something that isn’t connected with an example of measurable outcomes.

Big hat, no cattle no longer has its place in many places for UX. We have to change that.

I’ve argued before that much of what we ship are tool-shaped objects: artifacts that produce the feeling of work without doing the work, the readout written before the research, the deck that persuades a room of something that is untrue. The pitch taught designers that persuading the room is the work, when the work is what happens after everyone leaves it.

That confusion is expensive. A team can win every review, ship a beautiful thing, and move a metric not at all — and in a pitch culture nobody notices, because the metric was never the point. Output over outcome.

The point was the moment the lights came up and the client nodded.

You can hear the reflex in how designers describe their careers: the portfolio is a highlight reel of reveals created before the work was really done, not a record of outcomes.

The agency taught us to sell design so well that we forgot selling it was the easy part.

Clients Over Users

Every agency has an account man. In Mad Men he is Pete Campbell — smooth, ambitious, forever managing the client’s feelings so the creative work can survive contact with the person paying for it.

The account model is not a villain; it is a structure, and the structure has a fixed center of gravity: the client, not the user. The account exists to keep the client happy, because the client is the one who renews.

Marty Cagan drew the sharpest version of this distinction with missionaries versus mercenaries. Mercenaries build what they are told; missionaries own the problem and will argue with you about it.

Agencies are structurally mercenary — not because agency people lack conviction, but because the business model rewards delivering what the client asked for, on time, on budget, on brief.

Agencies are structurally mercenary; they serve the person who signs the check, and the user is whoever the client says the user is.

UX carried that reflex in-house and never quite set it down.

We still call the loudest stakeholder “the business,” still treat a vice president’s hunch as a requirement, still ship the thing that was asked for and quietly file the research that disagreed in a place it cannot be discovered. The account model trained us to confuse client service with design — to believe a satisfied room means a solved problem. The two come apart more often than we admit.

The client can be delighted and the user still stuck.

Someone in the room has to be loyal to the person who never gets a seat at the table, and agency culture never hired for that job.

Deliverables Over Outcomes

Agencies sell campaigns. The campaign is the unit of work — the thing that gets scoped, invoiced, presented, and, this is the key part, handed over. The agency ships the deliverable and moves to the next account. Whether the campaign worked is somebody else’s problem, measured after the invoice clears, if it is measured at all.

That model came into product design almost intact.

We scoped deliverables: the user journey, the workshop, the wireframe, the redline, the design system component, the handoff, the work about the work that wasn’t really the work. We measured ourselves by what we produced rather than by what changed, which struggles to survive in the world of AI.

It’s a world worth of portfolio reviews for how we measure today, even when we know the numbers in their portfolio are falsified to get past the interview panel.

John Cutler named it when he described the feature factory — teams that ship and ship and ship with no measurement other than the number of features shipped rather than delivered outcomes. You can invoice a deliverable; you cannot invoice an outcome in this model, so the agency learned to sell the thing it could bill for.

Design inherited that invoice, which is why so many teams can show you a gorgeous artifact and go quiet when you ask what it moved or if it even can be shipped. The deliverable is finished and photogenic; the outcome is slow and often disappointing in impact.

The same research that found top design performers pulling away from their peers points the other direction entirely: measure design with the rigor of revenue and business outcomes, and iterate with users until the outcome is real.

This is the opposite of ship-and-leave.

Auteurs Over “The System”

Don Draper was a genius, and that is the problem.

Agency culture organizes itself around the auteur — the singular creative whose taste is the product, whose name in on the door, whose persona wins the account, whose gut overrules the room. It is a seductive model and a fragile one, because it puts everything load-bearing inside one person’s head.

UX imported the auteur wholesale.

We built a star system: the rockstar designer, the portfolio shot with 40,000 likes, the award-show reel, the dribble portfolio, the presentation that talks about what we haven’t delivered, the person who puts together a framework that he wants to develop only as his own, the designer that want to own the design of the entire enterprise suite without regard to the team they work with.

We taught junior designers that the goal is to become the taste, to be the one whose judgment is trusted without evidence, to be them the one to blame the usability test for the choice.

In doing that, we quietly devalued the least glamorous and most durable work in the discipline — the systems, the documentation, and the shared components that let a hundred people design consistently without the genius in the room.

A system outlives the genius, and that is exactly why the genius culture was never in a hurry to build one that could stand the test of time

Brad Frost’s atomic design made the counter-case concrete: build systems, not pages — small, shared, maintainable parts anyone on the team can assemble, so quality stops depending on who happens to be in the meeting.

The above is so made for the world AI it’s laughable.

Great ideas can come from everyone and collaboration is more important than a designer’s ego when everyone touches the presentation, or the lead that doesn’t trust anything other their work and won’t let others in for feedback which shows a lack of respect for peers in their organization, and consequently the system that makes the company profitable. It is craft distributed for alignment, removing a single point of failure, replaces ego, and survives a resignation. It is craft with collaboration.

The auteur model resists this because a good system makes the auteur optional, the one thing the star was hired never to be.

The boring work goes undone, the knowledge stays trapped in one designer’s taste, and the team relearns the same lessons every time that designer leaves.

We need to change that.

The Churn Erased Institutional Memory

Agencies run on churn.

Accounts turn over, staff turn over, and the new-business engine never stops — there is always a pitch for the next logo, because last year’s logo is already someone else’s problem who bid lower for the account. It is a model built for movement, and movement is the enemy of memory.

Nobody stays long enough to remember what the last team already learned and that rhythm is poison for true research and discovery.

Teresa Torres makes the case in Continuous Discovery Habits that discovery is a weekly practice rather than a one-time project — a team talking to customers every week, building an understanding that compounds. It’s a true learning mindset where the collective knowledge of the organization every time someone talks to a user.

The agency cadence is the reverse: research is a phase you buy at the start of an engagement, run once, present, and never touch again. When the engagement ends, the learning walks out with the freelancers.

We have to work together and learn how not to compete with our co-workers in this new builder world — everyone will get credit if there is true alignment. That’s the goal.

Continuous discovery is a habit you keep so you can be better together over the long run, and churn is how organizations forget everything they paid to learn.

In-house UX absorbed the project shape even without the agency’s excuse for it. We reorganize, set ridiculous boundaries where we freeze out co-workers, we re-scope, and we shuffle designers between squads like a game of musical chairs so they don’t learn the domain and every reshuffle resets the clock on what the team knows about its users. Like an agency.

The cost stays invisible until you look for it.

It shows up as the same usability problem or video rediscovered three times in two years, the persona nobody trusts because nobody remembers making it or even taping it to the wall, and the research repository that quietly becomes a graveyard.

Institutions that cannot remember cannot improve, they only churn.

Draper sold nostalgia as the pain of an old wound, and that is the fair register for this argument too.

Agency culture is not a monster to be slain, it’s what we need to reform: It gave UX its craft, its vocabulary, and its seat at the business table, and plenty of us learned everything we know inside one and now we have to unlearn some of the habits.

The point is not to burn Sterling Cooper down; it is to notice which of its habits we kept without ever deciding to while making sure we should.

Practice design instead of performing it, and measure what the work moved rather than how the reveal landed. Serve the user over the client when the two pull apart, and be the person in the room loyal to whoever has no seat at the table.

The lights come up eventually, but the only question that matters is whether anything real is still standing in the room when they do.

title: Aunt Dolly Was Enough
text:
Aunt Dolly Was Enough

In the depths of sorrow, we turn to music. I know what each of my heartbreaks have sounded like. I know every song that has picked me up off the bathroom floor and every artist whose voice has been the unknowing soundtrack to my grief — due to loss, love, and everything in between. Those sonic moments of comfort — the ones that reach through the speakers and whisper that your loneliness isn’t singular — are so personal, shared between you, your headphones, and your tears. Dolly Parton has been with me for some heavy shit stuff (censored out of respect to Dolly, who hated cursing). Fittingly, since she couldn’t have kids of her own, Parton has helped me through my own journey with infertility. After my first pregnancy loss, I’d go on long walks by myself to cry, scream at the trees or God or whoever was listening, and grieve. I listened to a lot of Dolly (and Whitney and Aretha and all the divas whose voices have transcended their time on earth). What I remember most about those walks was that I listened to the WNYC podcast series Dolly Parton’s America.

In it, host Jad Abumrad walks listeners through Parton’s impact, from her poor Appalachian upbringing to her country roots and Dolly iconography to how borderless her influence became — how the themes of her folk music stretched from Appalachia to West Africa, from “Nashville to Nairobi”, the show charts Parton’s global appeal. Like many have pointed out since her death this week, Parton was the last thing we all agreed on. She was universally beloved when the concept of being “universally beloved” doesn’t really exist anymore. She was an elder who adapted to the times when so many of her generation reject change. She was a celebrity who spoke her mind and loudly stood up for the less fortunate when stars of that ilk are becoming increasingly rare. She was a rich white lady who could have been a billionaire and chose to be a philanthropist instead. She led with empathy. Now, being empathetic is denigrated as a weakness. She embraced her femininity while being fiercely feminist, proving the two aren’t mutually exclusive. She said she wasn’t political but her actions showed us her politics clearly. Parton wasn’t perfect and she held multiple contradictions at once, but there was one thing she was, unequivocally: good. 

That goodness stretched from Parton’s Imagination Library, which provided hundreds of millions of books to children, to her support for LGBTQ+ and Black communities, to how she carried herself, to her philosophies on life and the cards it dealt her. Oftentimes, we value women by our reproductive systems. Society will say that motherhood is where we show our worth, that a woman’s most virtuous achievement in life is giving birth. None of that is true, of course, but even in death, when Parton is being remembered for her vulnerable songwriting, unmatched artistry, impeccable comedic timing, and her many charitable contributions, we’re also talking about the fact that she had no biological children. It’s a conversation we wouldn’t be having if she were a man (case in point: we’re not talking about the late Tim Curry, who also passed this week, in the same way), which makes it unfair to a point, but I also think that Parton’s views on motherhood are important to excavate. She spoke about motherhood the same way she did life: with irreverent honesty, wit, wisdom, and humility. 

There isn’t much in the Dolly Parton’s America podcast about Parton’s struggle to conceive — she and her husband Carl tried for years — and her ultimate decision to be at peace with never having children, so there are quotes of her talking about her views on motherhood that I hadn’t seen until now that our timelines are full of Dolly Parton tributes, like this one she said to Andy Warhol for Interview Magazine:

“I couldn’t have children, I tried to for years. I’ve never been pregnant in my life. When I was a girl and fooling around, I was scared to death I’d get pregnant, and then when I got married and wanted to have children, I couldn’t have any. But I don’t miss it. I did for awhile, but I realize that I am everybody’s mother. I’ve raised five of my younger brothers and sisters, and now their kids call me Aunt Grannie. I’m like the grandma and the aunt.”

Last week, for the third time, a positive pregnancy test made me believe I’d finally become a mother. Once again, it didn’t work out the way I wanted. Despite growing up going to church, I don’t pray much anymore. What could possibly be the divine reasoning for the harrowing highs and lows of infertility? My husband and I are still trying, but over the past few days, I’ve been reckoning with the idea that it may not happen for us, that maybe I will never carry a pregnancy to term and raise a child who inherits a big forehead like all of us Newmans on my mom’s side of the family have. Parton has picked me up off the bathroom floor a lot this week. I’ve been inconsolable. Turns out, the third time wasn’t a charm. That fact has been a devastating reconciliation of expectations versus reality.

So much of the social media surrounding fertility journeys show the happy ending. There’s the hard fought battle for a baby, but it always ends with a baby. For Parton, it didn’t. And somewhere along the way, she and her husband decided that was for the best. She decided that providing books to hundreds of thousands of children was enough. She decided that helping raise her younger brothers and sisters was enough. She decided that being Aunt Dolly (most famously, to her goddaughter Miley Cyrus) was enough. A godmother, an auntie, a philanthropist, a caregiver. It was all enough. 

In the past week, many writers have taken on the impossible task of eulogizing a last-of-her-kind icon who cannot be put into words. How do you describe the defeat, hurt and humor laced in the melodies of “Jolene”? How do you explain the spiritual experience of listening to “Light of a Clear Blue Morning” for the first time? How do you illustrate that Parton was the closest thing we had to an actual saint on earth while also being a complex cultural figure who loved to tell a dirty joke? How do you sum up that she birthed every country female singer songwriter currently reigning the charts? When Ashley Fetters Maloy from The Washington Post tried to tribute Parton, her piece “Why it matters that Dolly Parton wasn’t a mother” was met with backlash. People took offense to the publication’s post on X that read, “Parton’s lack of children demonstrated that the world could in fact love a woman who wasn’t a mother.. She was proof that a person could be an advocate for children while choosing against parenting.”

I actually understand and agree with Fetters Maloy’s sentiment about how the world sees women. See: when JD Vance disparaged “childless cat ladies” or how the internet reacts when a woman dares to get pregnant past the age of 40 or, god forbid, decides not to have children at all and expresses zero regret for that choice (Oprah and Tracee Ellis Ross may be applauded now but they have faced an onslaught of judgment). And with the tradwife movement on the rise, choosing to be childfree is radical. The whole piece is worth a read, not just the poorly-worded social post. Maybe it is a nice narrative to push though, that Parton was a progressive badass who chose to be childfree decades before it was cool, and in true Dolly fashion, there are cheeky quotes to back up that framing (“We don’t want children of our own… we don’t want the total responsibility” Parton told the BBC in 1978), but the reality is more complicated. Parton suffered from endometriosis resulting in a partial hysterectomy. She was unable to have children of her own, then chose not to become a parent by other means, and devoted her life to helping kids anyway, and raising them in her own way. I think it does Parton’s story a disservice to leave out the fact that infertility isn’t a choice, and that she spent years dealing with the devastating disappointment of a dream unrealized. 

“God has a plan for everything,” Parton said on the Today show in October 2017. “I think it probably was his plan for me not to have kids so everybody’s kids could be mine. And they are now.”

These quotes have been hitting me in the gut. I had an appointment at a new fertility clinic on Wednesday. It was scheduled months ago. I didn’t know when I booked it that I would be dealing with another unsuccessful pregnancy, or that Dolly Parton would be dead. When I walked in, “9 to 5” was playing on the speakers in the brightly lit office. As my doctor rattled off my medical history from her notes (including a fibroid removal surgery last year I am still mentally and physically recovering from), I listened to the faded sounds of Parton’s iconic anti-capitalist hit: “They let you dream just to watch ’em shatter/ You’re just a step on the bossman’s ladder/ But you’ve got dreams he’ll never take away.”

Infertility will have you questioning every choice you’ve ever made, especially ones that involved putting your career above starting a family, wondering why you spent years pouring cups of ambition, striving for titles that don’t mean much to you anymore. Some of that is just the web of bullshit grief spins in your brain, scrambling your sense of self, but, in that moment, I found it fitting that Parton’s pro-union pop masterpiece was playing in the background. Like Parton, I am an auntie and it’s the title I am most proud of. I have four perfect nieces and nephews (the youngest just turned six), and I’m grateful to be a surrogate auntie to my friends’ kids. I know that I have so much space in my heart for the children in my life, and if the maternal love I have to give goes to my community instead of a biological kid of my own, I think I can be OK with that — just like Parton was.

When I shared the above Parton and Andy Warhol quote on social media, the post (which has over 800,000 views and 83,000 likes) was flooded with comments affirming Parton’s status as a mother to the world and some testimonies from people whose aunts helped raise them. “I had a great aunt like this and she was and is one of the most important people in my life,” one commenter wrote. “The most motherly person in my family is an aunt of mine who has no children,” posted another.  

I have friends who have chosen to never have kids and they are some of the most caring, nurturing, and loving people I know. My own godmother, my mom’s best friend of almost 50 years, raised me just as much as my parents and big brothers did. She’s a striking, loud, Caribbean lady from St. Vincent who would never be caught without dark lipstick. She showed up to my cousin’s funeral with purple lips, head-to-toe polka dots and a wide brimmed fascinator. She taught me to dress boldly (I still raid her closet for bright prints and statement jewelry), to live fearlessly (she once stopped a mugger by whacking him with her purse), and how to be a loyal friend (my mom wouldn’t have survived my parents’ divorce without her). My godmother has kids of her own, but I’ve always felt like hers. I know intimately that you don’t have to give birth to someone to become their favorite person. And yet, I needed the reminder this week. I needed to remember that for all the years I was uncertain about having children, I knew that being an Auntie — by blood or through friendship — was the honor of a lifetime. Thinking of the women in my life who are nurturing kids who will grow up and write comments like the ones above made me replace sobs with happy tears. 

In death, Parton has provided me with something I didn’t think was possible a few days ago: hope. Not the hope that precedes the certainty of getting what I want, but hope that one day I’ll be able to accept whatever happens. Dolly Parton didn’t have her own kids, but that doesn’t really matter. She was a mother. In every sense of the word, she was maternal. Since the announcement of Parton’s death on Tuesday, stories of her generosity have filled our timelines. To millions of kids, she was the lady who sent them books. To her niece Rebecca Ann Seaver, she was her “most trusted confidant” and “best friend.” To Cyrus, she was “an angel.” Parton knew what it meant to value community, and to be a part of the village that raises a child. The most impressive thing about Parton wasn’t just that her music connected her to the world, it’s that her life was a testament to the value of kindness and community, to treating every child as your own, and to seeing humanity in everyone and knowing that empathy is our greatest strength.

Dolly Parton and I have the same birthday, over 40 years apart. A big-haired, big tittied, spunky blonde from Appalachia and an anxious, small chested Black girl from the suburbs of Ontario, Canada don’t have much in common on paper, but the fellow Capricorn was one of those fixtures in pop culture who felt like family. That may be a little parasocial, and I’m sure I’ve been projecting the trauma of my infertility onto her this past week, but sometimes, that’s what art and celebrity does. What we consume can be a mirror that reflects more about ourselves than the artist. Projection or not, I know that Dolly Parton’s legacy — more than the Grammys, the chart topping hits, and Oscar-nominated roles — will be that she was a good person doing good in the world. I may never be able to be a mom, but I can be good. I can try my best to use my privileges to benefit others. I can provide the children in my life and beyond with all the love, protection, and respect I can muster, just like Aunt Dolly.

title: Your Horoscope This Week: August 30 To September 5
text:
Your Horoscope This Week: August 30 To September 5

R29 babes, you made it through the eclipse threshold, and this week is about slowing down enough to understand what just changed. In the days after the Pisces lunar eclipse, emotions may still be settling and certain realizations may need time before they make complete sense. As August ends, Jupiter in Leo forms a supportive fire trine with Saturn in Aries, bringing the planet of luck and expansion into harmony with the planet of discipline and responsibility. This is the universe reminding us that bold dreams and practical effort can exist in the same room, and that the work we’ve been doing is creating real protection around the next chapter. Opportunities may feel more solid, confidence may return, and something that once felt risky could suddenly seem much more possible. Take the win, cosmic beings. You survived the emotional group project, and now the cosmos is handing everyone snacks.

The beginning of September is relatively calm, with no major transits until the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini on September 4th. Last Quarter Moons are checkpoints of release and recalibration, helping us decide what still matters after the Full Moon’s revelations and what can be left behind. A week ago, we were deep in our feelings; now the Gemini Moon offers perspective, peaceful detachment, curiosity, and enough playfulness to remember that one difficult chapter does not have to become our entire personality. Laugh when you can, and let yourself view the eclipse story from a little farther back. What a difference a week can make.

Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Aries Sun & Rising:

Aries, August ends with the kind of cosmic support that helps you remember what happens when confidence and discipline work together. Jupiter in Leo is energizing your romance, creativity, fame, fate, and inner child realm while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in your sign, making it easier to turn inspiration into something real. The ideas, risks, relationships, or creative goals that survived eclipse season now have stronger foundations beneath them. Put yourself out there, accept the invitation, share the work, or make the first move. You don’t need to choose between being bold and being responsible this week; the more seriously you take your joy, the more momentum it can create.

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini activates your communication and mindset zone, helping you process everything that shifted over the past week. A conversation, thought pattern, or piece of information may look very different now that the emotional intensity of the Pisces eclipse has settled. Let go of the need to explain yourself perfectly, replay every exchange, or turn one uncertain moment into a permanent conclusion. The Gemini Moon brings perspective, so change your mind where needed and choose the words that create movement instead of keeping you stuck in the same mental loop.

Taurus Sun & Rising:

Taurus, August ends by helping you strengthen your inner foundation before making your next move. Jupiter in Leo is expanding your home, family, roots, and emotional security realm while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in your solitude and closure zone. This can bring progress around a move, family decision, healing process, or the private work you’ve been doing to feel safer within yourself. You may finally understand that creating a better home life also requires releasing old fears, guilt, or habits that keep you emotionally stuck. Clear out a room, set a boundary with family, rest without apologizing for it, or make one concrete decision that gives your future self more peace.

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini activates your money and security sector, helping you reassess what’s actually worth your time, energy, and spending after eclipse season. A financial concern may feel less overwhelming once you look at it with fresh eyes, or you may realize that one expense, subscription, or income plan no longer makes sense. Review your budget, follow up on a payment, sell what you no longer use, or brainstorm a more flexible way to earn. The Gemini Moon wants options, so release the belief that there is only one path to stability and let yourself experiment with a smarter one.

Gemini Sun & Rising:

Gemini, you made it through eclipse season, and August ends by reminding you that your voice can open doors when the right people are listening. Jupiter in Leo is expanding your communication, writing, learning, and media realm while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in your friendship, community, and social network zone. A conversation, introduction, collaboration, or idea shared online could lead somewhere substantial now, especially if you have been consistent about showing up and refining your message. The vibe is less “crying in the notes app” and more “wait, this could actually work.”

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in your sign helps you step back and recognize how much you’ve changed since last week’s Pisces eclipse. You may feel ready to release an identity, expectation, look, habit, or personal storyline that no longer fits, especially if you have been shape-shifting to keep everyone else comfortable. Gemini energy gives you permission to update the narrative without turning it into a full press conference. Keep what still feels true, let the rest expire, and enter the weekend with more curiosity about who you’re becoming than attachment to who you used to be.

Cancer Sun & Rising:

Cancer, you made it through this month’s eclipses, and August ends with real momentum around money, purpose, and the career structure you’ve been building. Jupiter in Leo is expanding your income and security realm while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in your career and public image zone. This can look like a financial opportunity becoming more stable, a professional decision finally making sense, or greater confidence in what your work is worth. Use this week to take one serious step toward the income level you keep envisioning. The emotional fog’s lifting, and the universe is saying “okay, now let’s make it sustainable.”

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini moves through your spirituality, closure, and subconscious realm, giving you space to process everything the Pisces eclipse stirred up. You may notice that one fear, regret, or mental loop has less power over you than it did a week ago. Release the need to find a perfect explanation for every feeling, and give yourself permission to rest, journal, pray, unplug, or sit in silence without turning solitude into isolation. The Gemini Moon helps you loosen your grip on the story and keep only the lesson.

Leo Sun & Rising:

Leo, you made it through eclipse season, and August ends with your confidence returning alongside a much clearer sense of where you’re headed next. Jupiter in your sign is expanding your identity, visibility, and personal goals while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in your travel, education, publishing, and expansion realm. A bold idea can start feeling much more realistic now because you’re finally willing to give it structure. The universe is supporting the version of you who dreams big and also reads the fine print, which is growth.

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini activates your friendship, community, and social network zone, helping you reassess who belongs in this next chapter. One week after the Pisces eclipse, you may have more perspective on which friendships feel reciprocal, which group dynamics have become distracting, and where you’ve been seeking approval from people who aren’t even paying that much attention. Use this week to clear out the stale group chats, follow up with the collaborators who inspire you, and release the pressure to be everywhere at once. Your next era needs community, Leo, but it does not need an audience of random spectators.

Virgo Sun & Rising:

Virgo, how does it feel to come through the final eclipse of the year during your own birthday season and realize that you’re entering this new chapter with a very different understanding of yourself? Jupiter in Leo is expanding your spirituality, healing, and behind-the-scenes realm while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in your intimacy, transformation, and shared-resources zone. This can help you make sense of the emotional, financial, or relational weight you’ve been carrying and see where greater trust, structure, or support is finally becoming possible. You may feel ready to close out an old fear, become more intentional about what you share with others, or make a private decision that strengthens your sense of inner stability.

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini brings a checkpoint to your career, reputation, and long-term goals. One week after the Pisces eclipse may have shifted your perspective on relationships, you could now feel more aware of how much your public life has been shaped by trying to meet everyone else’s expectations. This weekend may leave you wanting to rethink the way you present yourself professionally, refine a goal that has become too rigid, or step away from a role that no longer reflects who you’re becoming. Give yourself room to experiment with a new direction and let clarity build through movement.

Libra Sun & Rising:

Libra, now that you’re on the other side of the Pisces eclipse, you may be realizing just how much your daily life affects the way you show up in relationships, work, and even your own body. Jupiter in Leo’s expanding your friendship, community, and long-term goals realm while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in your partnership zone, creating a rare sense that the right people can actually help you build something lasting. A friendship may become more serious, a collaboration may begin to feel reliable, or a relationship could start aligning more naturally with the future you want. This is a strong moment to notice who follows through, who brings substance to your ideas, and where support is becoming mutual instead of symbolic.

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini moves through your travel, education, publishing, and expansion zone, helping you step back from the emotional intensity of the past week and look at the bigger picture. You may find yourself reconsidering a trip, course, belief, or long-term plan, especially if it was shaped by pressure rather than curiosity. This weekend is less about locking in one grand answer and more about letting your perspective become flexible again, so give yourself room to explore, ask different questions, and remember that changing your mind can be part of moving forward.

Scorpio Sun & Rising:

Scorpio, now that the Pisces eclipse has stirred your heart, creativity, and inner child, the end of August helps you turn what you felt into something you can actually build. Jupiter in Leo’s expanding your career, visibility, and long-term ambitions while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in the area of wellness and daily responsibility. This can bring a rare sense that your professional growth is no longer competing with the structure your life requires; the two can begin supporting each other. A goal that once felt too large may now seem achievable because you can finally see the practical steps between where you are and where you want to be.

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini moves through your intimacy, shared-resources, and transformation realm, helping you gain perspective on an emotional or financial entanglement that felt heavier during eclipse week. You may find yourself reconsidering what you owe, what you share, how much access someone has to you, or whether a bond still feels reciprocal beneath the intensity. Gemini energy gives you enough distance to talk through what’s been difficult to name and consider more than one solution, rather than assuming everything must end in a dramatic all-or-nothing decision. Let the weekend show you where a lighter agreement, clearer boundary, or more honest conversation could release pressure without requiring you to shut down.

Sagittarius Sun & Rising:

Sagittarius, the emotional weight of the Pisces eclipse may still be settling, especially around home, family, or your sense of belonging, but the end of August helps you remember that your life is still expanding beyond what feels uncertain right now. Jupiter in Leo is energizing your zone of travel, education, and long-term vision while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in your creativity, romance, and inner child realm. This is a beautiful reminder that your biggest dreams can become more real when you give them shape, discipline, and time. You may feel called to recommit to a creative project, take a romantic risk with greater maturity, or finally treat an idea you love like something worth building rather than something you visit only when inspiration strikes.

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini moves through your partnership zone, helping you look at your closest relationships with more perspective and less emotional fog. One week after the eclipse may have brought up questions about where you feel at home and who helps create that feeling with you, this weekend could lead to an important conversation about expectations, reciprocity, or the future of a bond. You may also notice that you’re ready to release the need for every relationship
to fit one fixed definition. Let curiosity guide the conversation, listen for what’s changed, and allow the connection to evolve without forcing an immediate verdict.

Capricorn Sun & Rising:

Capricorn, the Pisces eclipse may have left you with a lot to think about, but the end of August gives you a much stronger sense of what needs to be handled privately before you can move forward with confidence. Jupiter in Leo is expanding your intimacy, shared-resources, and transformation realm while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in your home, family, and emotional foundation zone. This can help you make meaningful progress around a shared financial plan, a housing decision, a family responsibility, or a deeper conversation about trust and support. You may realize that the stability you want cannot come only from holding everything together by yourself. The more honest you are about the support you need, the easier it becomes to build a life that feels secure on every level.

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini moves through your work, wellness, and daily routine realm, helping you release some of the pressure that’s accumulated around being productive all the time. You may find yourself wanting to reorganize your schedule, rethink how much you take on in a single day, or create more flexibility around habits that have become too rigid to be useful. This weekend’s a good time to notice where your routine supports your energy and where it simply keeps you busy, because the lighter Gemini influence can help you find a smarter way forward without turning every adjustment into another serious life overhaul.

Aquarius Sun & Rising:

Aquarius, the Pisces eclipse may have brought a financial or self-worth realization that’s still settling, but the end of August reminds you that the right relationships can help you move forward with much more confidence. Jupiter in Leo is expanding your partnership realm while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in your communication zone, making this an excellent time for honest conversations that lead somewhere constructive. A romantic partner, collaborator, client, or close friend may help you clarify an idea, strengthen a commitment, or see a possibility you had been too overwhelmed to recognize during eclipse week.

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini moves through your creativity, romance, fate, and inner child realm, bringing a lighter checkpoint after such an emotionally charged month. You may realize that a crush, creative project, or personal dream has become burdened by too many expectations, and this weekend gives you permission to reconnect with the original spark that made it exciting. Let yourself experiment without needing every idea to become a business plan or every romantic interaction to become a life decision. The more playfully you approach what comes next, the easier it’ll be to recognize which desires still feel alive and which ones you’re ready to release.

Pisces Sun & Rising:

Pisces, last week’s lunar eclipse in your sign may have left you feeling like you shed an entire version of yourself overnight, and the end of August helps you understand what this rebirth is asking you to build next. Jupiter in Leo is expanding your work, wellness, and daily routine zone while forming a supportive trine with Saturn in Aries in your money, security, and self-worth sector. This is the kind of energy that helps you turn a personal realization into a more sustainable life, whether that means creating healthier habits, asking for better pay, restructuring your workload, or becoming more disciplined about where your time and energy go. You may still feel emotionally tender, but this alignment reminds you that small, responsible choices can protect the new version of you that eclipse season just revealed.

Then, on September 4th, the Last Quarter Moon in Gemini moves through your home, family, and roots realm, helping you reassess what you need to feel emotionally safe and supported. You may find yourself wanting to change your space, have a family conversation, release an old childhood narrative, or become more honest about where you no longer feel at home. Gemini energy brings perspective, so you don’t have to make every feeling mean that your whole foundation is falling apart. Let yourself consider new ways of creating belonging, and allow home to become something flexible enough to grow with you.

title: R29 Editors Are Obsessing Over Lululemon Bags—These Are, Hands Down, The Best
text:
R29 Editors Are Obsessing Over Lululemon Bags—These Are, Hands Down, The Best

Lululemon knows a thing or two about creating viral belt bags, chic travel accessories, and conversation-starting tote bags. The R29 reader-favorite brand also knows how to do them especially well, with most bag styles receiving at least 4 out of 5 stars from thousands of devout customers.

And there’s a whole lot of range and variety. From sporty fanny packs and versatile crossbody bags to spacious carryalls and backpacks, Lululemon has all your everyday essentials… and concert outfit and vacation plan needs covered!

Read on to shop bag styles from Lululemon’s bestsellers, as well as in-demand new arrivals with already-stellar reviews.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Lululemon Backpacks

A trusty backpack is essential for any fitness or everyday wardrobe — and Lululemon has a variety of high-quality packs to choose from. “For years, Lululemon’s Everyday Backpack was my go-to travel pack,” R29’s senior writer Karina Hoshikawa says. “The design is sleek and streamlined, but don’t be fooled: The backpack can hold a ton of stuff. I also love that it has plenty of compartments and pockets (but not too many that things inevitably get lost), and has a padded pocket that fits my 15-inch work laptop. It’s also made from a water-repellent, recycled nylon fabric that is surprisingly easy to clean in case of accidental spills. I use it mostly for travel, but I truly could see this working perfectly for everyday use (hence the name), commutes, or school.”

For fans of the beloved Everywhere Belt Bag, don’t sleep on its sibling, the spacious Everywhere Backpack: It’s a classic style, with durable ripstop fabric (not to mention, 100% of the polyester is recycled material). Heading out for a hike or long bike ride? The highly rated All Sport Backpack is ready for any outdoor adventure, with plenty of space for gear and hydration. Or, for something a bit more versatile, the Wunderlust Backpack Mini is a great pick. 

Shop Lululemon Bags

DashDividers_1_500x100

Lululemon Travel & Gym Bags

Many of Lululemon’s larger bags — including the viral Big-Ass design — have found their way into our best-of-the-best travel bag and gym bag roundups, so we had to highlight them first. Hoshikawa has called the 2-in-1 Travel Duffle Backpack “a game-changer” because of just how roomy and convertible it is. But the smaller City Essentials Bag is also roomy and just as popular with shoppers for gym runs and weekend trips.

Shop Lululemon Bags

DashDividers_1_500x100

Lululemon Crossbody Bags

A trusty crossbody bag is a must-have, and Lululemon has several customer-favorite styles to pick from. Take on the concert and club circuit with the new All Night Festival Bag or the bestselling Crossbody Camera Bag, which R29’s former senior life writer, Tanyel Mustafa, has in black and takes out clubbing. And for your travel plans, long hikes, and every adventure in between, choose from the brand’s popular Wunderlust collection. They’re all as versatile and functional as they are stylish.

Shop Lululemon Bags

DashDividers_1_500x100

Lululemon Tote Bags

Lululemon offers a tote bag for every occasion and need. Opt for the roomy Daily Multi-Pocket Tote to carry around your everyday essentials. Hoshikawa owns this style in the logo design and uses it for day trips and office days. The brand also has totes specifically designed for travel (lightweight and water-repellent) and for new parents (with water bottle holders and an attached changing mats). You’ll even find structured canvas totes in 12L or a 9L size, which could serve as a lunch bag.

Shop Lululemon Bags

DashDividers_1_500x100

Lululemon Belt Bags

The Everywhere Belt Bag is no doubt the most well-known and beloved Lululemon bag out there, with the original 1L size and style averaging a 4.7 star rating from over 23,300 customers. For many people, the sleek fanny-pack-meets-sling-bag style has become a closet staple for running errands, attending concerts, or traveling. Because of its popularity, there are now many iterations of the belt bag, from extra large and extra mini sizes to clear bags, perfect for concerts and baseball games. The brand also offers additional belt bag styles if you’re looking for something off the beaten path.

title: I Tried GapStudio’s Fall Denim-Forward Collection—& I Have Thoughts
text:
I Tried GapStudio’s Fall Denim-Forward Collection—& I Have Thoughts

I’m a self-declared Gap girl, so I was super eager to preview GapStudio‘s fall collection, which launches today. The premium clothing line under Gap and Zac Posen’s direction has entered its second fall season with a capsule of elevated denim, matching sets, workwear, and wardrobe essentials. “It’s a natural evolution of the language we’ve been building at GapStudio, but this season, we pushed proportion and construction much further,” Posen tells Refinery29.

The new womenswear and menswear collections unsurprisingly complement each other, both inspired by turn-of-the-century American workwear, according to Posen. “The collection is inherently gender-fluid. I was interested in creating a shared wardrobe where menswear and womenswear inform one another and the pieces can move naturally between the two,” he adds. “Ultimately, it’s about giving people beautifully considered clothes with a strong point of view and the freedom to create their own character through them.”

Ahead, I try the GapStudio womenswear collection and share my honest opinions about the look, feel, and sizing of the limited-edition pieces so you can confidently cart up your favorites (before they sell out) and build trendy fall outfits.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Crop Canvas Jacket, Belted Utility Pants & Poplin Fitted Shirt

Cutting right to the chase, this deep indigo matching set was my absolute favorite and is my top recommendation to cart up. It’s especially great if you’re petite and curvy since GapStudio only offers standard sizing and lengths, and us shorties want to get in on the action!

I was completely shocked when this set felt like it was tailored to my body. “Seaming, volume, and structure are built into the architecture of the garments, so the construction becomes part of their character and the way they sit on the body,” Posen explains. As a curvy gal (currently with a 33-inch waist and 46-inch hips), it can be hard to find pants that fit right in all the right places. But these ones did, with a size 31/12 cinching my waist even before tightening the matching belt. And standing at just 5 feet and 3 inches tall, I surprisingly wasn’t swallowed by the wide-leg pants, especially when paired with a wedge.

The matching jacket similarly fit great in a size large, and I found the cropped proportion to be very flattering both when worn opened or buttoned up. It gives the vibe of an elevated denim jacket, and as a whole outfit, a Canadian tuxedo, sans any denim (but more on that below!).

I also really loved pairing the pants with this button-down top, which was my favorite top of the collection. The fitted torso hugged my waist and felt more feminine than a typical button-down top. Plus, the exaggerated puffed sleeves added more dimension and extra interest to an otherwise (let’s face it, boring) wardrobe staple.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Printed Denim Sweatshirt & Pleated Parachute Pants

It took me quite a few glances when previewing images of this sweatshirt online to realize that it was in fact a sweatshirt and not a denim jacket. Posen notes: “There are playful moments of trompe l’oeil inspired by archival Gap pieces, taking something incredibly familiar and shifting the perception of it through print, fabrication, and construction.” And after a fascination with faux-denim sweatpants in the last few years, I foresee this piece going viral too. The distressed denim wash and nearly-metallic button prints were trippy in all the best ways. The heavy fabric and oversized fit were also super comfortable — I opted for a size large again.

I paired the top with cargo-inspired parachute pants. These were definitely more snug and required some serious maneuvering over my hips because of a slimmer waistband. There are adjustable straps and buckles on both sides that allow you to adjust the waist and customize to your comfort level. But even so, I think sizing up to a 14 would have been better. Overall, I really enjoyed the utilitarian-style buckles, oversized back pockets, and adjustable cinched hems of these pants.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Double-Pocket Denim Jacket & High Rise Pintuck Jeans

Though it was hard for Posen to pick his favorite GapStudio pieces, he shares: “I love the full denim-on-denim look with the Pintuck Flare Jean and Double Pocket Jacket.”

This elevated Canadian tuxedo definitely made a statement, though it did feel too big for me. With a different sizing chart, I opted for the size 33/16R, which did fit my waist and hips (though with some back gaping), but the flared fit was too long for little ol’ me, pooling around my feet, even in heels. But I can see these becoming a tall-girl approved jean! I really appreciated the elevated front and back pintucks and the super-flattering seams above the back pockets for an exaggerated hourglass shape.

The matching jacket was very cool with its oversized balloon sleeves, front patch pockets, and collar. The versatile dual-ended zipper also allows for re-styling the piece in many ways. But I think because of the baggy fit and XL details, I would’ve preferred to size down to a medium. (Hot tip: It’s also great to layer with the sheer mesh denim printed tee.)

DashDividers_1_500x100

Printed Denim Terry Dress

Yet another deceiving look that impressed me! No, this is not a denim dress, but rather a French terry dress with a hyper-realistic denim print. The size large was perfect for me thanks to the super stretchy fabric. This style may just be the fashion It-girl alternative to wearing a sweater dress this fall. It also feels smart enough to wear to the office without anyone blinking an eye.

So, if you’re ready to add to cart and just need some more styling inspo, Posen suggests: “Mix pieces across menswear and womenswear, layer unexpected shapes together, or put something more architectural against something incredibly familiar. There shouldn’t be too many rules. Clothes are a tool for self-invention.”
